title: Revisiting Machine Learning for Healthcare Provider Fraud Detection: Volume Baselines and Data Leakage
content: Supervised learning for healthcare provider fraud detection is frequently benchmarked on a public Kaggle dataset of inpatient and outpatient claims with provider-level fraud labels. We re-examine this benchmark under a controlled, reproducible protocol and ask three questions: how much do standard classifiers add over a trivial baseline, how sensitive are model rankings to thresholding conventions, and how do claim-level formulations and random splits affect reported performance. Using 5,410 providers (9.35% labelled potentially fraudulent) and 558,211 claims, we evaluate logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM with five-times-repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Ranking providers by their total reimbursed amount, with no training at all, attains a ROC-AUC of \( 0.938\pm0.009 \) and a PR-AUC of \( 0.688\pm0.033 \), within one standard deviation of all four trained models (ROC-AUC 0.932--0.943; PR-AUC 0.664–0.695). Model rankings by F1 at the default 0.5 threshold change when class weighting is switched on, although ROC-AUC changes by at most 0.003. When provider labels are propagated to individual claims, claim-level features alone are nearly uninformative for unseen providers (ROC-AUC \( \approx0.53 \)), whereas adding provider-level context under a random claim-level split yields near-perfect tree-ensemble scores (ROC-AUC \( \geq0.9998 \)) that fall to about 0.93 under provider-grouped splitting. We recommend that results on this benchmark be reported with provider-grouped evaluation, threshold-free and budget-based metrics with variability across repeated splits, and a billing-volume baseline.
